Democrats flipped a first U.S. Senate seat in early midterm election results that boosted their push to win control of Congress in what would be a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump.
Also read: U.S. Midterm Election night agenda: When polls close and when to expect results
Popular Democratic former governor Roy Cooper defeated Mr. Trump’s handpicked candidate for the Senate in North Carolina, while rising Democratic star Jon Ossoff won re-election to the Senate in Georgia, according to media projections.
Also read: Trump’s Republicans scramble to stop Democratic midterms wave
Polls opened on Tuesday (November 3, 2026) in the U.S. midterm elections , starting with Vermont and several other East Coast States, including New York, New Jersey, Virginia and Kentucky. The vote will decide how much power President Donald Trump has for the rest of his term. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 of the 100 Senate seats, and governorships in 36 States are up for election, with about 210 million people registered to vote.
Democrats will wrest control of the U.S. House of Representatives from Republicans, media projections showed -- a seismic shift that will spell confrontation for the second half of President Donald Trump’s term.
Democrats notched a string of early victories in U.S. midterm elections Tuesday, flipping a Republican-held Senate seat and making inroads in conservative House districts as President Donald Trump faced the prospect of a bruising election setback.
Democrats gain ground in U.S. midterms as Trump battles bruising setbacks and Georgia’s governor race reshapes the political landscape.
Democrat Rebecca ‌Bennett defeated U.S. Representative Tom Kean ⁠of New Jersey, according to media, flipping a Republican-held ‌seat.
Mr. Kean was the most vulnerable Republican in ‌New Jersey’s congressional delegation. He flipped the Democratic-held seat in 2022 ‌but disappeared from the public for months ⁠in an election year before disclosing ‌this summer his battle with depression.
The mood inside the White House is “defiant” despite Democrats notching early victories in a blow to President Donald Trump, a White House official told AFP .
“The White House mood is defiant,” the official said on condition of anonymity, saying that Mr. Trump would stop the “radical left” no matter what the results were and warning: “Buckle up.”
Indian American Pia Dandiya won the election to the U.S. House of Representatives from Florida’s 22nd congressional district, defeating Casey Askar, a Marine veteran.
Ms. Dandiya, a former high school principal, bagged 51.9% of the votes to become the newest Indian-American U.S. congresswoman, as per the results declared.
Her opponent Mr. Askar, polled 49.1% of the votes. Pia Dandiya, first-generation Indian-American, wins U.S. House of Representatives from Florida Pia Dandiya wins Florida’s 22nd, becoming a 1st-gen Indian-American congresswoman with 51.9% of votes.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, was elected governor of the state of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected to that office in the United States, media projections showed.
Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, who ran as a Republican. Current Governor Brian Kemp is term-limited and could not run again.
Suhas Subramanyam, who served as an advisor to President Barack Obama, has been re-elected as a member of the U.S. House of Representatives.
Mr. Subramanyam, 40, won from Virginia’s 10th congressional district, polling over 61.5% of the vote against Republican Dave Beckwith, who managed to win 36.4% of the ballots cast.
Born in Houston to Indian parents, took lessons of service while attending college at Tulane University in New Orleans, where he helped organise volunteers to rebuild the communities affected by Hurricane Katrina. Suhas Subramanyam re-elected as U.S. Congressman from Virginia Democrat Suhas Subramanyam wins re-election to the US House from Virginia's 10th district, highlighting his bipartisan service and Obama-era policy roles.
Roy Cooper, a well-known former two-term Governor, ‌defeated a hand-picked candidate of President Donald Trump after campaigning ‌on the high cost ‌of ⁠food and energy as ⁠Mr. Trump’s approval ratings fell U.S. midterm elections: Democrat Roy Cooper flips Republican-held US Senate seat in North Carolina Democrat Roy Cooper wins North Carolina's Senate race, flipping a Republican seat amid high costs debates and Trump-era tensions.
Democrat Chris Pappas won New Hampshire’s open U.S. Senate seat, according to media projections, defeating ‌Republican John Sununu and preserving a crucial Democratic seat as the party fights to take control of the chamber.
Mr. Pappas’ victory denied Republicans a pickup in the cold-weather state, where ⁠high energy prices had become a major issue amid President Donald Trump’s war with Iran. He will succeed Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, who is retiring after 18 years.
While the 39-year-old Jon Ossoff has said that he has “zero interest in running for President,” his victory in Georgia bolsters his status in the Democratic Party two years before the next presidential vote.
Americans voted in the most consequential midterm elections, which early surveys predicted as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, signalling a mood for change.
Over 210 million Americans were eligible to vote in the elections, which began at 6.00 am eastern time on Tuesday (November 3, 2026) for 435 seats of the U.S. House of Representatives, 37 seats of the U.S. Senate, 36 posts of state governors and a slew of local public offices.
Polling was over in Indiana and Kentucky at 6.00 p.m. eastern time on Tuesday (4.30 a.m. India time Wednesday) and would close in a staggered manner till past midnight across different time zones in the U.S..
The first polling stations closed Tuesday in the U.S. midterm elections, with Democrats hoping to secure control of Congress and the future of President Donald Trump’s agenda in the balance.
Parts of Indiana and Kentucky were the first to shut polling places at 6:00 pm (2300 GMT). At stake in the midterms are all 435 seats in the House, one-third of the Senate, and a slew of state and local positions.
Wall Street stocks finished mostly higher as oil prices continued to pull back while markets awaited results from U.S. midterm elections that could reshape President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.
Crude prices, which fell sharply on Monday on revived talk of U.S.-Iran peace prospects, fell modestly hours after Trump insisted that a deal with Tehran “could happen,” with traders also citing unconfirmed West Asia media reports saying progress on Iran’s nuclear program and frozen funds had been made.
The prospect of easing energy costs helped Wall Street steady after several sessions of losses, in particular on the tech-heavy Nasdaq, which enjoyed a positive session after three straight declines.
Linda Jones has set up a folding chair near a polling station in Atlanta, Georgia, to watch out for anything that might keep people from casting their ballots in the U.S. midterms.
“I want to help people navigate the voting, which has gotten more and more complicated,” said the septuagenarian, who is serving as an election observer for the first time.
She and two other volunteers will keep a close watch on activity around this polling station, set up in a public library, and report any issues that arise.
“In a climate like we are in the country, there’s misinformation, there are actions that are taken that discourage some people from voting, certain parts of the population,” she said.
In the hours before polls opened for the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, federal judges issued a series of rulings restricting the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to pressure state election ⁠officials over alleged noncitizen voting.
Over the past several months, as President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans geared up to defend their majorities in both houses of Congress, the administration ramped up a crackdown on noncitizen voting, which Mr. Trump allies say is a ‌major problem even though evidence suggests it is exceedingly rare.
That push has repeatedly encountered resistance in the courts. Federal judges have found that the Trump administration was overstepping its authority by ‌wading into election administration, a responsibility that the U.S. Constitution assigns to the states, and that ‌lists ⁠it had generated of alleged noncitizens registered to vote were inaccurate and risked disenfranchising naturalised U.S. ⁠citizens.
Ballot machines malfunctioned in a hotly contested House race in New York state Tuesday, prompting right-wing influencers to fling unfounded allegations of U.S. midterms voter fraud even as local election officials insisted all ballots would be counted.
President Donald Trump and his allies have previously spread unproven claims about voting machines, alleging that they are faulty or unreliable.
The Westchester County Board of Elections said it was aware of an issue involving paper ballots that is preventing voting machines from accepting ballots at polling locations throughout the county.
The board “wants to reassure every voter that your vote matters, your ballot will be secure and your vote will be counted,” with ballots instead placed in emergency bags, it said in a statement.
On polling day, Donald Trump sprung a surprise by announcing that the U.S. will stop providing Israel USD four billion in aid from next year, which Democrat Ro Khanna described as a desperate attempt to stave off a “Blue tsunami”.
On the eve of the elections, the U.S. launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qesham island in the Hormuz Strait. Officials said that the strikes were in response to Iran firing at a U.S. aircraft.
U.S. rock legend Bruce Springsteen, a staunch Democrat, urged election officials Tuesday to resist any government voting interference amid fears President Donald Trump’s administration may intervene in the midterms.
“I’m speaking to election officials and representatives of our government on election day. You have sworn an oath to preserve, protect and defend our Constitution,” the 77-year-old said in a video on Instagram.
“That means you have a solemn duty to ensure that our votes are securely counted,” he said. “You who represent us must never consent to any directives that undermine our constitutional right to a free and fair election.”
“Our vote is our voice, and it’s up to you to ensure that our voice is heard,” added Springsteen, wearing a brown flannel shirt.
Europe’s benchmark equities index slipped on Tuesday, as doubts over a potential West Asia peace deal ⁠kept markets on edge ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, while investors also assessed a slew of earnings.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index closed 0.58% lower at 645.66 points, with mining ‌shares leading declines on weaker copper prices.
Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior ‌Iranian official told Reuters. Overnight, the United States carried out what it ‌called ⁠defensive strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island.
State officials who run U.S. elections are braced for possible intervention by President Donald Trump’s administration in Tuesday’s midterms -- fearing federal authorities could disrupt voting, challenge ballot counts or try to block unfavourable results.
Mr. Trump, whose Republicans face an uphill battle to keep control of Congress, has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections and urged his party to “nationalise” voting in at least 15 places.
The White House says it is protecting election security, and many of the feared scenarios remain hypothetical.
The U.S. Constitution gives the president no direct role in running elections, and courts have so far rebuffed the administration’s main legal challenges.
Three NASA astronauts, including Anil Menon, on Tuesday cast their ballots in the U.S. midterm elections from the International Space Station orbiting over 400 kms above Earth.
Mr. Menon and two other astronauts – Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins – filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to election officials.
“Yes, you can even vote from space,” Mr. Menon said in a post on X.
Mr. Menon reached the International Space Station on July 14 on board a Russian Soyuz mission. Delaney and Watkins reached the orbital laboratory on October 1 on board a SpaceX rocket.
“All three U.S. crew members had the privilege of voting from Space Station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials,” Mr. Menon said.
An Oklahoma City ‌man was charged with sending ⁠hundreds of threatening letters to ‌State election officials, lawmakers, ‌pollsters ‌and ⁠media organisations ahead ⁠of the midterm congressional election.
Robin Martin ‌was charged in U.S. District Court ‌in Oklahoma with conveying false or misleading ⁠information and hoaxes and mailing ‌threatening communications.
Powders in letters tested have been ‌determined to be either yeast or flour, ⁠the FBI ⁠said in an affidavit.
More than three dozen voting laws passed in Republican-controlled states are taking effect for the first time this year, many of them containing elements of proposals that Trump tried unsuccessfully to get through Congress.
At the state level, the changes include new requirements to show proof of citizenship. College students in New Hampshire won’t be using college IDs. Iowa voters without ID can’t count on other voters to vouch for them, and some voters in Mississippi might need birth certificates or passports for verification.
Naturalized citizens might get to polling places and learn they’ve been purged because databases used to check their citizenship against voter registration lists are outdated.
A state-by-state guide to when polls close in the 2026 US midterm elections, key races to watch and when vote counts may be completed.
Voters in Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., are considering candidates for mayor aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America.
If Nithya Raman captures the mayoralty in LA and Janeese Lewis George wins in Washington, the two cities would follow New York’s lead, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor in 2025 after promising to transform city government to restore power to the working class.
US President Donald Trump said Tuesday (November 3, 2026), that Republicans would perform “better than you think” in the midterm elections.
He declared that “inflation is solved” and “everything’s going good”, despite continued voter concerns over the cost of groceries, fuel and healthcare.
Inflation is running at 3.7% annually, up from 3% when Mr. Trump began his second term. In an interview with Fox & Friends, Mr. Trump did not address concerns over prices, instead highlighting immigration enforcement and expanding US manufacturing.
Democrat James Talarico is making an ambitious bid to win a Texas Senate seat for his party for the first time since 1988.
He is challenging Republican Ken Paxton, whose record has been marked by ethical questions and a statehouse impeachment over corruption allegations.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said higher fuel prices are linked to the conflict in Iran and urged Republicans to be honest with voters. He said blaming former President Joe Biden for the increase would amount to “gaslighting” working-class people.
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces an unusually strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who has made affordability a key issue.
A Democrat has not won a Senate race in Kansas in 94 years, and the contest has set a state record for campaign advertising spending.
Susan Myers (60), a voter in Falmouth, said she is hopeful that Democrat Troy Jackson can defeat Republican Sen. Susan Collins, but wary after recent disappointments.
“I feel like there’s been so much disappointment these last few election cycles that I don’t want to get my hopes up,” she said.
Iowa’s top of the ticket is up for grabs after Republican Governor Kim Reynolds and Senator Joni Ernst opted out of reelection bids.
In the governor’s race, Democrat Rob Sand faces Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer who won the primary over a Trump-endorsed congressman. In the Senate race, Democrat Josh Turek is up against Republican Ashley Hinson, who is endorsed by Mr. Trump.
Latinos helped return Donald Trump to the White House in 2024 and are poised to play an outsized role in today’s midterms (November 3, 2026). The path to a U.S. House majority runs through heavily Latino districts in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida and Texas, and the Senate race in Texas could also hinge on them.
About 6 in 10 Hispanic adults disapprove of Mr. Trump’s handling of the presidency, an AP-NORC poll from October found.
The U.S. Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s push for California to set aside thousands of disputed mail ballots ahead of the midterms, AP reported.
Stock markets struggled on Tuesday (November 3, 2026) after another AI-fuelled tech selloff on Wall Street, as investors turned to the US midterms. Seoul’s Kospi fell 3.6% as SK hynix and Samsung tumbled, and London, Paris and Frankfurt were lower. Tokyo was closed for a holiday.
Brent crude rose 1.7% to $106.58 a barrel after US media reported limited US strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, following a drop of more than 7% on Monday on hopes of US-Iran talks.
Polls close at 11 p.m. ET (9.30 a.m. IST) in California and Washington, where voting is mainly by mail. Ballots postmarked by Election Day will be counted if received by November 10, 2026, in California and November 23 in Washington. In 2024, about 38% of California’s vote and 33% of Washington’s was uncounted on election night.
Polls close in Hawaii and most of Alaska at midnight, and the final polls at 1 a.m. in the Aleutian Islands. In Alaska, the bulk of mail results are not expected before November 18.
Polls in 15 states close at 9 p.m. ET (7.30 a.m. IST), including Arizona, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin.
Arizona does not begin releasing results until 10 p.m. Michigan was the slowest of these in 2024, reaching 90% counted at 4.50 a.m. Key races include Senate contests in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas. At 10 p.m., polls close in Montana, Nevada and Utah.
Polls fully or partially close in almost half the states at 8 p.m. ET (6.30 a.m. IST), including Florida, Maine, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. In 2024, Florida’s count was 90% complete by 8.07 p.m., while Maine did not reach the halfway mark until 12.54 a.m.
Polls in almost all of Michigan and Texas also close at 8 p.m., but statewide winners will not be declared until the final polls close at 9 p.m. Key races include Senate contests in Florida, Maine and New Hampshire, and governor races in Florida and Pennsylvania.
The first polls close at 6 p.m. ET (4.30 a.m. IST on Wednesday, November 4, 2026) in most of Indiana and Kentucky, but no statewide winners will be declared until the last polls close at 7 p.m. All polls close at 7 p.m. in six states, including Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia, which tend to finish most counting on election night. North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close at 7.30 p.m.
Most Florida polls close at 7 p.m., but no statewide winners will be declared until 8 p.m. Key races include Senate contests in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio.
The first polls in several U.S. states on the East Coast opened just after 6 a.m. ET today (November 3, 2026). Polls have opened in New York, New Jersey, Virginia, Maine, Kentucky, Vermont, New Hampshire, Indiana and Connecticut.
The Associated Press reported that the midterm elections, which will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s second term, begin to come to a close today (November 3, 2026).
Americans are deciding whether to drastically shift power in Washington, angry over high prices and an unpopular war with Iran, it said.
